68ceb3ba125483f14a56326b.title: AI Based Social media site
68ceb3ba125483f14a56326b.description: Trying out the approach of having custom algorithms for each user using the llms and optimized search indexing and querying.
68ceb3ba125483f14a56326b.detailedContent:
##  Project Overview  
This project aims to build a **social media platform** with a unique feature:  
- Users can **describe in natural language** what kind of feed they want.  
- The system uses **LLMs + optimized search indexing and querying** to generate a **dynamic, personalized feed** that adapts to the user’s request.  
- This moves beyond static algorithms or generic personalization, giving users **direct control** over how their content is curated.  

---

##  Original Project Plan  

The project was designed to include the following phases:  

### **Phase 1 – Core Social Media Functionality**  
- User onboarding and authentication.  
- Basic profile setup and management.  
- Post creation and interactions (likes, comments, media upload).  

### **Phase 2 – Baseline Feed Framework**  
- Implement a simple feed (e.g., chronological or popularity-based).  
- Build indexing and querying mechanisms for content retrieval.  

### **Phase 3 – Natural Language Feed Customization**  
- Allow users to type in what kind of feed they want (e.g., “more fitness content,” “fewer political posts”).  
- LLM interprets the request → generates a query strategy → retrieves relevant posts.  
- Feed updates dynamically based on user instructions.  

### **Phase 4 – Advanced Personalization**  
- Continuous learning from user preferences and activity.  
- Support **multi-turn instructions** (refining the feed iteratively).  
- Balance personalization with diversity and discovery.  

### **Phase 5 – Scaling & Deployment**  
- Deploy the application on scalable infrastructure.  
- Optimize feed generation performance.  
- Add moderation, safety, and content filtering mechanisms.  

---

##  Progress So Far  

###  Implemented Features  
A **basic social media application** has been built as the foundation for testing the main feature. Current capabilities:  

-  **User Onboarding & Profiles**  
  - Registration, login, and profile management.  
  - **Email verification** for secure onboarding.  

-  **Posts Service**  
  - Users can create and share posts.  
  - Support for **media uploads** (images, videos).  

-  **Engagement Features**  
  - Likes and comments system.  
  - Interactive content sharing and feedback loop.  

This foundation is **scaled enough for testing** the upcoming **natural language feed customization feature**.  

---

##  Summary  

The project has already delivered the **core social media foundation** (onboarding, posts, likes, comments, and media support).  

The next step is to implement the **main differentiator**:  
- Users can **type in natural language what kind of feed they want**, and the platform will generate a **customized, dynamic feed** accordingly.

68ceb10e125483f14a563264.title: AI Induced E-commerce site
68ceb10e125483f14a563264.description: Trying out features for AI/LLM induced search, navigation and recommendation for E-commerce applications
68ceb10e125483f14a563264.detailedContent:
#  AI-Powered Multi-Modal Product Search  

##  Project Overview  
This project aims to build an **AI-driven product discovery platform** that allows users to search for products in a **human-like, intuitive way**. Instead of relying only on traditional keyword search, the system supports:  

- **Natural language search** → Users can describe what they need (even vaguely) and receive product suggestions.  
- **Image-based search** → Users can upload an image to find visually similar products or related categories.  
- **Hybrid understanding** → The AI bridges vague human descriptions or visual cues to the actual products available in the inventory.  

---

##  Original Project Plan  

At the start, the project was designed to include the following phases:  

### **Phase 1 – Core Search System**  
- Build **natural language query processing** using an LLM.  
- Enable **web search + product page extraction** for supplementing vague queries.  
- Connect processed results with the **local product database**.  

### **Phase 2 – Image Search Integration**  
- Use **Google Cloud Vision API** to extract labels, objects, and features from user-uploaded images.  
- Pass extracted features to the LLM to generate product category mappings.  
- Add **direct image similarity search** using open-source models.  

### **Phase 3 – Multi-Modal Fusion**  
- Combine image features and text descriptions to improve product recommendations.  
- Handle **ambiguous inputs** (e.g., “something cozy to wear at home” or uploading a vague lifestyle image).  

### **Phase 4 – User Interface (UI)**  
- Design and implement an **intuitive UI** supporting text input, image upload, and results display.  
- Add navigation features (categories, filters, sorting).  

### **Phase 5 – Deployment & Scaling**  
- Deploy application to a scalable cloud platform.  
- Optimize APIs and database queries for performance.  
- Add personalization features (user history, preferences).  

---

##  Progress So Far  

###  Implemented Features  
1. **Natural Language Search**  
   - Accepts vague/free-form queries.  
   - LLM reformulates queries into structured search.  
   - Performs **web search → product page parsing → local database matching**.  

2. **Image-Based Search (Vision API Integration)**  
   - Extracts attributes and objects from uploaded images using **Google Cloud Vision**.  
   - Converts extracted features into descriptive queries for the LLM.  
   - Maps results to available product categories.  

3. **Direct Image Similarity Search**  
   - Implemented using **open-source image embedding models**.  
   - Matches uploaded images with product images in the inventory.  

### ⚙️ Tech Stack  
- **OpenAI API** → Natural language understanding & query generation.  
- **Google Cloud Vision API** → Image feature extraction.  
- **Custom Web Scraper** → Retrieves product details for query matching.  
- **Open-source Image Models** → Embedding-based similarity search.  
- **Database (Inventory)** → Product categories and metadata.  

---

##  Upcoming Updates  

-  **Fully Functional UI** (interactive product browsing & hybrid search).  
-  **App Deployment** (cloud hosting & backend integration).  
-  **Search Optimization** (improved embeddings, faster query handling).  
-  **Enhanced Navigation** (filters, categories, personalization).  

---

##  Summary  

The project has successfully implemented its **core search engine** with **natural language and image-based queries**. By combining **LLMs, computer vision, and database matching**, we now have a foundation for a **multi-modal, intelligent product discovery platform**.  

The upcoming focus will be on **UI development, deployment, optimization, and navigation features**, eventually evolving into a **scalable e-commerce-ready solution**.

68ca0e86256ed334d872328c.title: AST-Guided Patch Generation
68ca0e86256ed334d872328c.description: It implements an end-to-end agent that locates, edits, and verifies code fixes for real GitHub issues (SWE-bench style) under strict constraints (no internet, open weights, ≤30 minutes per served issue).
68ca0e86256ed334d872328c.detailedContent:
Konwinski Prize — AST-Guided Patch Generation (Kaggle Competition)
1. Problem

The Kaggle Konwinski Prize competition challenged participants to design an AI agent capable of automatically fixing real GitHub issues (SWE-bench style).

Key constraints:

No internet access during scoring.

Open-source weights and code only.

≤ 30 minutes runtime per issue.

Submissions had to either:

Output a valid unified diff patch, or

Explicitly skip (since a wrong patch was penalized more than skipping).

  These constraints made the task extremely challenging, testing the ability to build a robust, conservative, end-to-end patching system under real-world limitations.

2. My Solution

I developed a multi-stage agent, implemented in a Kaggle notebook, to locate, edit, and verify code fixes safely. The approach combined LLMs with AST-guided context construction and strict validation to maximize correctness while minimizing false positives.

System Workflow:

Locate suspect lines — LLM extracts two literal code lines (error + preceding line).

Search & filter — grep repository for those lines, then apply adjacency filter (±1 line).

File selection — second LLM ranks and selects the most relevant files.

Context construction — AST-guided backward tracer gathers surrounding code, imports, definitions, and scopes.

Patch synthesis — LLM generates a unified diff patch.

Mechanical validation — verify patch format with unidiff parse + patch --dry-run.

Self-verification — multiple LLM judges vote Yes/No; majority approval is required.

Final decision — submit patch or safely skip if uncertain.

  The architecture was deliberately conservative:

Skipping > wrong fixes, in line with competition scoring rules.

3. Techniques & Approaches

Multi-agent LLM pipeline — separated roles (locator, selector, generator, judge) to reduce error compounding.

AST-guided context extraction — surgical backward tracing of definitions, imports, and scopes for compact yet high-signal prompts.

Unified diff generation & validation — enforced strict compliance with diff format + dry-run application.

Voting-based verification — redundancy through multiple LLM judges to reduce false positives.

Time & token budgeting — runtime tracking and token accounting to stay within 30 minutes/issue.

Skip logic — conservative design to maximize overall score by avoiding penalties.

4. Skills Demonstrated

AI/ML engineering — designing LLM-driven repair agents.

Program analysis — AST parsing, scope tracing, and dependency resolution.

Systems design — modular pipeline with safety checks and fallback logic.

Prompt engineering — precise, minimal, and robust prompt templates.

Software validation — enforcing patch correctness mechanically before submission.

Optimization under constraints — careful runtime and resource management.

5. Technologies Used

Python 3.11 — core implementation (competition runtime).

vLLM — efficient inference with open-weight LLMs.

unidiff + GNU patch — patch parsing and dry-run validation.

pandas / polars — structured logging and diagnostics.

ast (Python stdlib) — abstract syntax tree parsing for context tracing.

Kaggle evaluation API — issue streaming and scoring integration.

6. Impact

This project demonstrates how to build a production-style AI coding agent that can autonomously repair real-world repositories while respecting strict runtime and correctness constraints.

It highlights expertise in:

LLM orchestration

Software engineering

Program analysis

Optimization under constraints

Ultimately, it shows how competition-style challenges can evolve into practical AI-assisted tools for large-scale software maintenance.

Kaggle Notebook :

https://www.kaggle.com/code/charansv/konwinski-sub-2

#  Indian Stock Market & News Feature Factory — Modeling-Ready Parquet with 80+ Engineered Signals

> Build a modeling-ready market dataset by combining **equity price data** (NSE/BSE) with **news-driven sentiment** and engineered features.

This repo contains three modular notebooks plus concise docs that together form a reproducible pipeline:
1) **Equity data extraction** → 2) **News sentiment building** → 3) **Final dataset creation & feature engineering**.

---

## TL;DR

- **What this demonstrates**
  - Practical **ETL** for market data, **NLP** for daily sentiment, and **feature engineering** for ML.
  - Robustness: **failure logs**, **intermediate saves**, and **idempotent** steps.
  - Interpretability: a simple **linear model** to learn weights for a **composite sentiment feature**.
- **What you get**
  - A **final parquet** with technical indicators, market & macro series, lagged sentiment, and a weighted sentiment metric.
  - A **feature glossary** explaining every column.

---

## Repo Contents

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `equity data extraction.ipynb` | Extract NSE/BSE tickers and fetch historical OHLCV data; logs failures. |
| `sentiment_scores.ipynb` | Fetch financial news (RSS/GDELT), score with VADER, aggregate per company/day. |
| `Dataset creation main.ipynb` | Merge, clean, create lags, learn feature weights, and output the final dataset. (feature engineering for all the 80+ signals) |
| `equity data extraction documentation.md` | Documentation for the equity notebook. |
| `sentiment scores creation documentation.md` | Documentation for the sentiment notebook. |
| `main dataset creation documention.md` | Documentation for the final dataset notebook. |
| `final features.md` | One-line description of **every** final dataset column. |

> Tip: Docs are short and skimmable. Start with **`main dataset creation documention.md`** and **`final features.md`**.

---

## Pipeline Overview

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[BhavCopy CSVs + NSE_tickers.csv + bse_tickers.csv] --> B[equity data extraction.ipynb]
  B -->|OHLCV per ticker + failure logs| C[sentiment_scores.ipynb]
  C -->|daily sentiment per company| D[Dataset creation main.ipynb]
  D -->|feature weights + final parquet| E[[merged_with_weighted_sentiment_final.parquet]]
  D --> F[(feature_weights_final.csv)]

68cc58c2125483f14a563251.title: ClusterGAN for Regime Discovery on Indian Stocks (NSE)
68cc58c2125483f14a563251.description: I adapted ClusterGAN to unlabeled NSE stock data to discover market regimes directly from high-dimensional features (OHLCV, indicators, sentiment, macro, global indices, FX/commodities). I trained G/D/E with WGAN-GP and latent consistency, swept latent std & clipping, explored cluster counts K ∈ [2, 100], and compared against K-Means.
68cc58c2125483f14a563251.detailedContent:
# ClusterGAN for Regime Discovery on Indian Stocks (NSE)  

##  Objective  
The objective of this project was to **adapt the ClusterGAN paper** for unlabeled **NSE stock data** and test whether it can **discover latent market regimes** directly from high-dimensional features.  
Specifically, I wanted to see:  
- Whether ClusterGAN could uncover **interpretable regimes** aligned with technical/macro/sentiment signals.  
- Whether it would also reveal **latent “mysterious” regimes** driven by exogenous shocks not captured in features — useful for risk detection and alerts.  

---

##  Project Overview  
Most published ClusterGAN applications focus on “nice” labeled benchmarks like MNIST. In contrast, **financial markets are unlabeled, non-stationary, fat-tailed, and regime-shifting**.  

This project used a **large consolidated NSE dataset (~518,000 rows × 92 features)** engineered by me, including:  
- **Core OHLCV & technical indicators** (RSI, MACD, Bollinger Bands, ATR, SMA/EMA/WMA, etc.).  
- **Momentum & volatility features** (rolling std, Sharpe ratio, ROC, Z-scores, kurtosis/skewness).  
- **Lagged & rolling features** (returns, prices, volumes).  
- **Sentiment signals** (news sentiment, lagged scores, weighted sentiment metric).  
- **Market/global indices** (Nifty50, SP500, FTSE100, DAX, Nikkei225).  
- **Macro & risk proxies** (USD/INR, crude oil, gold, VIX).  

The goal was to run **ClusterGAN sweeps across K=2–100**, test stability knobs (noise std σ, latent clipping), and benchmark against **K-Means clustering**.  

---

##  The Problem  
- Traditional clustering (K-Means, hierarchical) struggles on **non-stationary, fat-tailed financial data**.  
- Market regimes are often **partially explainable**: some linked to volatility/technical states, others driven by **news or macro shocks**.  
- Needed a method that could capture **both interpretable and latent structures**.  

---

##  The Solution  
- Implemented **ClusterGAN with WGAN-GP + latent consistency** (MSE for continuous z_n, CE for discrete z_c).  
- Used **MLPs** for G/D/E for tabular stability.  
- Preprocessed with **MinMax scaling [−1,1]**, company-aware splits, and NaN/inf handling.  
- Swept over:  
  - **Cluster counts (K)** → {3, 7, 100}.  
  - **Noise std (σ)** → 0.05–0.25.  
  - **Clipping ranges** → [−0.6, 0.6], [−0.7, 0.7], [−0.8, 0.8].  
- Benchmarked against **K-Means** with same K.  
- Added **post-hoc explainability check** (Random Forest / LightGBM predicting cluster IDs) to distinguish explainable vs latent regimes.  

---

##  Techniques & Approaches  
- **GAN architecture**: Generator, Discriminator, Encoder with WGAN-GP loss.  
- **Latent design**: mixed code z = [z_n (Gaussian), z_c (one-hot cluster ID)].  
- **Training**:  
  - Adam optimizer (5e-5, betas=0.5,0.9).  
  - Batch size up to 10k.  
  - Sweeps with short runs (8 epochs).  
- **Evaluation metrics**: Silhouette, Calinski–Harabasz, Davies–Bouldin, Compactness, Inertia.  
- **Explainability check**: trained classifiers to see if clusters were predictable from features.  

---

##  Key Results  
- **K=7 run**:  
  - **4 clusters** were highly explainable from features (clear technical/momentum/volatility regimes).  
  - **3 clusters (~10% of data)** were “mysterious/volatile” — not explainable by current features, but systematically formed → likely exogenous shocks (macro/news).  
- **Best stability knobs**:  
  - Noise std σ ≈ **0.10–0.15**.  
  - Clipping ≈ **[−0.6, 0.6]**.  
- **Representative metrics (K=7, one run)**:  
  - Silhouette ≈ 0.00 (sampled 45k points).  
  - CH ≈ 34,680.8.  
  - DB ≈ 2.95.  
  - Inertia ≈ 2.8M.  
- **Extreme K tests**:  
  - K=3 → coarse but interpretable regimes.  
  - K=100 → fragmented; required longer training/regularization.  

 **Conclusion**: ClusterGAN discovered both interpretable market regimes and latent “volatile” clusters likely tied to **exogenous drivers** missing in current features.  

---

##  My Contributions & Skills Demonstrated  
- Adapted **ClusterGAN** to large-scale, high-dimensional financial tabular data.  
- Engineered **92 features** across technical, macro, sentiment, and volatility dimensions.  
- Designed **systematic sweeps** over cluster counts, noise, and clipping.  
- Implemented **robust preprocessing pipeline** (NaN/inf handling, scaling, company-aware splits).  
- Conducted **explainability diagnostics** (tree classifiers on clusters).  
- Interpreted results in terms of **market regimes and exogenous shocks**.  

---

## ⚙️ Technologies Used  
- **Python** (NumPy, Pandas, Scikit-learn, Polars)  
- **PyTorch** (GAN implementation: G/D/E)  
- **GAN framework**: WGAN-GP + latent consistency  
- **LightGBM / Random Forest** for explainability checks  
- **Visualization**: Matplotlib, Seaborn  
- **Data sources**: NSE, Yahoo Finance, sentiment pipelines, macro/commodity/FX series  

---

##  Future Work  
- **Strengthen z_n** → richer intra-cluster variations by adjusting loss weights.  
- **Full K sweep (2–100)** with multiple seeds + temporal robustness.  
- **Add more exogenous signals** → earnings events, macro calendars, sectoral indices.  
- **Company embeddings** → capture cross-asset similarities while retaining idiosyncrasies.  
- **Downstream usage**:  
  - Regime-aware forecasting with LightGBM/Transformers using cluster ID.  
  - Risk alerts when samples map to low-density latent regions.  
- **Longer training & deeper nets** → improve separation and stability.  

---

##  Impact  
This project shows that **ClusterGAN can uncover latent regimes in Indian stock markets**, including both interpretable clusters (technical/momentum/volatility regimes) and **hidden “volatile” states** not explained by standard features.  
Such latent regimes are valuable for **risk management, regime-aware forecasting, and alerting systems**, and highlight the need for integrating **macro & event-driven features** in future pipelines.  

Notebook:
https://www.kaggle.com/code/charansv/stock-cluster-gan-1

68ceca01acdda27e835d5321.title: Research paper text extraction for finetuning
68ceca01acdda27e835d5321.description: This was used only for private educational and research purposes and never redistributed.
68ceca01acdda27e835d5321.detailedContent:
#  Research Papers Dataset — Notebook Docs 

### Notebooks
- **`Research publishings extraction.ipynb`** — discovers papers and collects **metadata**, **PDF/HTML links**, and **raw text** (when permitted).
- **`512-data-extraction.ipynb`** — cleans, normalizes, and **chunks** text (≈512-token windows) to create **training-ready JSONL** for open-source LLM fine-tuning.

### What they do (at a glance)

1. **Discover & Collect**
   - Query research indexes/publisher pages for target topics/keywords.
   - Respect `robots.txt`, apply polite **rate limits** and retries.
   - Store metadata: `paper_id`, `title`, `authors`, `year`, `venue`, `doi`, `url`, `pdf_url`, `license?`, `abstract`.

2. **Fetch & Parse**
   - Download HTML/PDF **only when allowed**.
   - Parse HTML (BeautifulSoup) or PDF (pdfminer/pymupdf) → plain text.
   - Normalize whitespace; optionally strip boilerplate (headers/footers/references).

3. **Validate & Deduplicate**
   - Drop duplicates by **DOI** or hash of `(title+authors+year)`.
   - Filter corrupted/short texts; keep language of interest (e.g., `en`).

4. **Clean & Segment (512-data-extraction)**
   - Section-aware splitting when possible (Abstract, Intro, Methods, …).
   - Tokenize and **chunk to ~512 tokens** with small overlaps to preserve context.
   - Add provenance fields (`source`, `crawl_time`, `checksum`, `source_license`).

5. **Save Training Files**
   - **Pretraining style**: one `text` field per chunk.  
   - **Optional SFT formats** (if you generate targets): e.g., summarization or QA tuples.
   - Outputs:
     - `papers_raw.jsonl` — metadata + raw text (per paper)
     - `papers_clean.jsonl` — cleaned text + normalized metadata
     - `papers_chunks.jsonl` — chunked text for training
     - *(optional)* task-specific JSONL for SFT

68cc5728125483f14a563244.title: Multi-Horizon Stock Forecasting
68cc5728125483f14a563244.description: I created a large-scale stock market dataset covering almost all NSE-listed companies with daily data and over 80 engineered features spanning technical indicators, sentiment, macroeconomic, and global signals. Using this dataset, I built predictive models (LightGBM, early Transformer prototypes) and multi-horizon forecasts, while also simulating trades with realistic backtesting. The project provides a robust foundation for future hybrid ensemble models, portfolio optimization, and reinforcement learning–based trading strategies.
68cc5728125483f14a563244.detailedContent:
# NSE Stock Dataset Creation, Predictive Modeling & Trade Simulation  

##  Objective  
The objective of this project was to **create an extensive real-world stock market dataset** covering almost all **NSE-listed companies (daily data)**, engineer **80+ rich features** spanning technical, macroeconomic, sentiment, and statistical signals, and then use this dataset for downstream experiments such as **predictive modeling** and **trade simulation**.  

The project also set out to **test a hybrid ensemble approach** combining **LightGBM (tabular patterns)** and **Transformers (temporal patterns)**. While resource limitations prevented full deployment of this ensemble at scale, it remains part of the **future pipeline**.  

---

##  Project Overview  
The workflow was divided into **three main components**:  

1. **Dataset Creation & Feature Engineering**  
   - Extracted historical daily stock data for almost all NSE companies (and BSE tickers for completeness).  
   - Engineered **80+ features** across categories:  
     - **Technical indicators** (RSI, MACD, Bollinger Bands, ATR, etc.)  
     - **Volatility & momentum features** (rolling std, rate of change, momentum, acceleration).  
     - **Lagged & rolling features** (lagged prices/volumes, rolling returns, rolling Sharpe ratios).  
     - **Pattern features** (candlesticks, Fibonacci retracements, pivot points).  
     - **Market & global indicators** (Nifty50, SP500, FTSE100, Nikkei225, DAX, INR/USD, crude oil, gold, VIX).  
     - **Macroeconomic signals** (exchange rates, inflation proxies, commodity levels).  
     - **Sentiment features**:  
       - Collected daily financial news from **Reuters, Bloomberg, Economic Times, WSJ, GDELT**.  
       - Scored with **VADER sentiment analysis**.  
       - Created **lagged sentiment features (1, 5, 10 days)**.  
       - Learned a **Weighted Sentiment Metric** via regression coefficients.  

2. **Predictive Modeling**  
   - Tested **LightGBM** for tabular feature-based forecasting.  
   - Prototyped **Transformer-based models** to capture temporal dependencies.  
   - Designed an **ensemble (LightGBM + Transformer)** pipeline to combine feature-wise and temporal patterns (future implementation).  
   - Forecasting tasks:  
     - **Single-step predictions** (next-day returns/movements).  
     - **Multi-horizon forecasting** (10-day ahead prices with LightGBM).  

3. **Trade Simulation**  
   - Built a **backtesting environment** with:  
     - Transaction costs & slippage.  
     - Stop-loss/take-profit mechanisms.  
     - Position sizing rules.  
   - Evaluated strategies using **PnL, Sharpe ratio, max drawdown, and win/loss rates**.  

---

##  The Problem  
- Public stock datasets are usually raw (just OHLCV) and lack engineered signals.  
- No unified dataset combining **technical, sentiment, macro, and market-wide features** existed for NSE companies.  
- Predictive models often fail in real-world backtesting without **macro and sentiment conditioning**.  
- Ensemble approaches combining **tabular ML (trees)** and **sequence models (Transformers)** are underexplored in finance.  

---

##  The Solution  
- **Built a feature-rich dataset** (~80+ engineered features × hundreds of NSE companies × multi-year coverage).  
- Integrated **macro + global indicators** and **daily news sentiment pipelines** into company-level stock data.  
- Trained and compared:  
  - **LightGBM** → strong baseline for feature-driven tabular patterns.  
  - **Transformers** → sequence modeling of temporal dependencies.  
  - **LightGBM + Transformer ensemble (planned)** → hybrid approach balancing feature-wise and temporal insights.  
- Simulated **trading strategies** to validate predictive models against realistic market conditions.  

---

##  Techniques & Approaches  
- **Data ingestion**: Ticker extraction, Yahoo Finance API, BhavCopy parsing for NSE/BSE.  
- **Feature engineering**: 80+ features across technical, sentiment, macro, volatility, and rolling statistics.  
- **Sentiment analysis**: VADER, lagged features, Weighted Sentiment Metric.  
- **Modeling**: LightGBM, Transformers, planned ensemble pipeline.  
- **Forecasting**: single-step + 10-day multi-horizon with LightGBM.  
- **Backtesting**: custom trade simulation with realistic costs.  
- **Evaluation**:  
  - Predictive → RMSE, MAPE, Accuracy, AUC.  
  - Trading → Sharpe ratio, drawdowns, PnL.  

---

##  Key Results  
- **Dataset**: Daily data for almost all NSE companies with **80+ engineered features**.  
- **Multi-horizon forecasting (LightGBM)**:  
  - 1-day MAPE ≈ **5.9%**, increasing to ~**17%** by day 10.  
  - Short-horizon forecasts generalize well; errors grow with horizon length (expected in finance).  
- **LightGBM vs Transformer**:  
  - LightGBM delivered strong results on feature-driven tasks.  
  - Early Transformer experiments were limited (row-wise modeling only), highlighting the need for true sequence windowing.  
- **Trade simulation**:  
  - Feature-informed strategies outperformed naïve baselines.  
  - Profitability was sensitive to transaction costs and macro volatility regimes.  

 **Conclusion**: The dataset proved effective for both modeling and simulation. LightGBM excelled on tabular patterns, while Transformer potential remains for future sequence-based modeling.  

---

## My Contributions & Skills Demonstrated  
- Built a **large-scale financial dataset** covering almost the full NSE universe.  
- Engineered **80+ diverse features** (technical, macro, sentiment, volatility, rolling).  
- Designed a **sentiment pipeline** using financial news + VADER + lagged/weighted metrics.  
- Implemented **multi-model predictive experiments** (LightGBM, Transformer, hybrid pipeline design).  
- Developed a **trade simulation framework** with realistic execution constraints.  
- Balanced **data engineering, financial domain knowledge, and ML expertise**.  

---

##  Technologies Used  
- **Python** (Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, Polars)  
- **TA-Lib & custom scripts** for technical indicators  
- **LightGBM, XGBoost, PyTorch Transformers** for modeling  
- **Optuna** for hyperparameter tuning  
- **Backtesting**: custom Python simulation environment  
- **Sentiment**: VADER, RSS feeds, GDELT integration  
- **Macro & global data sources**: Yahoo Finance, RBI, IMF, FRED APIs  
- **Visualization**: Matplotlib, Seaborn, Plotly  

---

#  Bangalore Real Estate Data – Extraction Notebooks (Simple Documentation)

This short doc explains how the two notebooks extract Bangalore real-estate data from a **popular local realtor site** for research/internal analysis.

> Notebooks:
> - `Realtor url extraction.ipynb` — collects listing **detail page URLs** for selected Bangalore localities.
> - `realtor-dataset-creation.ipynb` — opens each URL and **scrapes structured fields**, then saves a clean dataset.

---

##  Prerequisites

- **Python** 3.9+
- **Drivers**: Firefox + `geckodriver` (or Chrome + `chromedriver` if you switch the driver)
- **Libraries**:
  - `selenium`, `bs4` (BeautifulSoup), `pandas`, `joblib`
  - Standard: `time`, `json`, `csv`, `os`, `random`
- (Optional) **Site login**: if the site gates some details behind login/OTP, configure environment variables instead of hardcoding:
  - `REALTOR_PHONE`, `REALTOR_EMAIL` (and handle OTP manually when prompted)

> **Ethics & Compliance**  
> - Respect the website’s **Terms of Service** and **robots.txt**.  
> - Use conservative rate limits and minimal request volume.  
> - Data is for **internal evaluation**/research; do not redistribute raw content.

---

## Notebook 1 — `Realtor url extraction.ipynb`

###  Goal
Collect property **detail page URLs** across key Bangalore localities to feed the second notebook.

###  What it does
1. **Driver setup**  
   Initializes a Selenium **Firefox** WebDriver (headless optional) and imports helper libs (`selenium`, `bs4`, `joblib`, etc.).

2. **(Optional) Login flow**  
   Some listing details can require login. The notebook contains a login block (via phone/email) using Selenium waits and basic form interactions.
   - Replace any hardcoded credentials with **environment variables**.
   - OTP entry is manual when prompted.

3. **Target localities**  
   Prepares a list of locality search URLs around Bangalore (e.g., **Yelahanka, Jayanagar, KR Puram, Indiranagar, Koramangala, HSR Layout, Electronic City, Whitefield, Marathahalli, Malleshwaram, Padmanabhanagara, Gandhinagar**).

4. **Pagination & URL capture**  
   - Visits each locality’s results page, iterates pages (or scrolls) with **explicit waits**.
   - Parses result cards (via CSS/XPath) and extracts the **property detail links**.
   - Deduplicates in memory; can periodically save with `joblib`/CSV.

5. **Output**  
   - Saves a clean list of detail URLs (e.g., `property_urls.json` or `urls.csv`) for the next notebook.

###  Notes & Tips
- Use **`WebDriverWait + EC`** (expected conditions) rather than fixed sleeps wherever possible.
- Add **randomized small delays** (`time.sleep(random.uniform(1.0, 2.5))`) to be polite and reduce blocking risk.
- If the site uses infinite scroll, send `END` key presses to load more cards before scraping.

---

## Notebook 2 — `realtor-dataset-creation.ipynb`

###  Goal
Open each detail page URL, extract **structured property attributes**, and build a **tabular dataset**.

###  What it does
1. **Driver & session management**
   - Initializes a Selenium driver (Firefox by default).
   - Rotates **User-Agents** across batches to reduce fingerprinting.
   - Processes URLs in **batches**, saving intermediate progress so a crash doesn’t lose work:
     - `property_data.json` — rolling snapshot of scraped records
     - `processed_urls.json` — set of URLs already processed

2. **Robust page loading**
   - Uses `WebDriverWait` on document/body and key elements.
   - Retries on **timeouts**, **stale elements**, or transient network issues.
   - Light scrolling and a small post-load delay to ensure dynamic elements render.

3. **Field extraction**
   Extracts a core set of fields (presence depends on the listing):
   - **Rent** (monthly), **Deposit**
   - **Total SqFt**
   - **Location** (neighbourhood / area text)
   - **Livability Score**, **Transit Score** (if shown on the site)
   - **URL** (source link)
   - Additional details captured by iterating **key–value blocks** on the page (e.g., property type, furnishing, floor, facing, bathrooms, parking, etc.) via stable CSS selectors.

   > Example selectors used (anonymized):  
   > - IDs: `#rent-maintenance`, `#square-ft`, `#emi`  
   > - Headings/labels & values: `h5.detail-key`, `h5.detail-value`  
   > - Scores/indicators: `[data-original-title*="Livability"] .score-value`

4. **Cleaning & normalization**
   - Strips currency symbols (`₹`), units (`/M`, commas), extra whitespace.
   - Converts numeric fields to `int/float` where possible.
   - Ensures consistent column names and fills missing values with `None`.

5. **Saving the dataset**
   - Consolidates all records to a `pandas.DataFrame`.
   - Writes final CSV: **`realtor_dataset.csv`**.
   - Keeps the JSON snapshot for audit/reprocessing.

###  Notes & Tips
- Keep selectors **as semantic as possible**; avoid brittle class-only strategies when the site obfuscates classes.
- If a field is missing, **catch `NoSuchElementException`** and store `None` to keep schema stable.
- Tune **batch size** and delays to balance speed vs. reliability.

---

68cc485a125483f14a56321a.title: Conventional + Custom GNN based auto encoders for fraud detection
68cc485a125483f14a56321a.description: Testing both conventional supervised learning techniques and unsupervised custom GNN-based autoencoders for credit-card fraud detection.
68cc485a125483f14a56321a.detailedContent:
# Credit Card Fraud Detection with Supervised Models & Custom GNN Autoencoders  

##  Objective  
The goal of this project was to **compare conventional supervised learning techniques with unsupervised custom GNN-based autoencoders** for **credit-card fraud detection**.  

Fraud datasets are **extremely imbalanced and noisy**. While supervised methods like **LightGBM** are strong baselines, the project explored whether **graph-based autoencoders** could learn geometry-aware embeddings from tabular data and naturally separate fraud from non-fraud transactions without labels.  

---

##  Project Overview  
Credit card fraud is a high-stakes application where missed detections cost businesses significantly, but false positives hurt customer trust. Traditional supervised methods achieve excellent accuracy but may not generalize under extreme imbalance.  

In this project, I:  
- Trained **Decision Trees and LightGBM** (with imbalance handling) as supervised baselines.  
- Built **KNN graphs** from transaction features and trained **custom GAT/GCN-based autoencoders**.  
- Clustered embeddings using **HDBSCAN and KMeans** to evaluate whether fraud forms distinct communities.  

The project demonstrates that **ClusterGCN autoencoders + HDBSCAN** yield near-binary separation of fraud vs non-fraud clusters, while **GAT autoencoders** highlight fraud-heavy micro-clusters.  

---

##  The Problem  
- Fraud datasets have **fraud rate ≈ 0.17%** → extreme class imbalance.  
- Supervised classifiers perform well, but require **resampling, threshold tuning, and cost-sensitive adjustments**.  
- Most fraud detection work on tabular data doesn’t leverage **graph structure**.  
- Key question: *Can GNN-based autoencoders uncover fraud communities in an unsupervised way?*  

---

##  The Solution  
Two independent experimental tracks were explored:  

1. **Supervised Track**  
   - Decision Tree (with and without oversampling).  
   - LightGBM (with SMOTE, `scale_pos_weight`, and threshold tuning).  
   - Evaluation with Precision, Recall, F1, and AUC focused on the fraud class.  

2. **Unsupervised Track (Custom GNN Autoencoders)**  
   - Construct KNN graphs (k = 5, 10) from standardized tabular features.  
   - Train GNN autoencoders:  
     - **GCN / ClusterGCN AE** → Laplacian smoothing, scalable mini-batching.  
     - **GAT AE** → Attention-based aggregation, capturing heterogeneous neighborhoods.  
   - Extract embeddings and cluster with **HDBSCAN** and **KMeans**.  
   - Assess cluster purity and fraud concentration.  

---

##  Techniques & Approaches  
- **Data preprocessing**: standardization, oversampling (SMOTE), careful train/test split (80/20).  
- **Supervised models**: handled imbalance with oversampling + class weights.  
- **Graph construction**: built KNN similarity graphs, optionally weighted with cosine similarity.  
- **Autoencoder training**: minimized reconstruction loss (MSE/MAE).  
- **Clustering**: compared HDBSCAN (density-based) with KMeans (k=2).  
- **Evaluation**: emphasized Recall, F1, AUC for fraud (minority) detection.  

---

##  Key Results  

### Supervised Track  
| Model | Accuracy | Precision (fraud) | Recall (fraud) | F1 | AUC |  
|-------|----------|--------------------|----------------|----|-----|  
| Decision Tree | 99.90% | 66.7% | 71.1% | 68.8% | — |  
| Decision Tree + Oversampling | 99.92% | 81.3% | 68.4% | 74.3% | — |  
| LightGBM (SMOTE + pos_weight) | 99.99% | 0.989 | 0.926 | 0.957 | 0.997 |  

 **Observation**: LightGBM dominates in the supervised setting, but requires careful **threshold tuning** (PR curve / cost-sensitive Fβ).  

---

### Unsupervised Track (GNN Autoencoders + Clustering)  
- **GAT AE + HDBSCAN** → Multiple micro-clusters, one with **51 fraud / 9 non-fraud** (strong fraud concentration).  
- **GCN / ClusterGCN AE + HDBSCAN** → Two large clusters with clear separation:  
  - Cluster A: ~56k non-fraud / 25 fraud (~99.96% non-fraud).  
  - Cluster B: 49 fraud / 8 non-fraud (~86% fraud).  
- **KMeans** → Less aligned than HDBSCAN (fraud diluted across clusters).  

 **Observation**: ClusterGCN + HDBSCAN provided a **clean near-binary fraud vs non-fraud split**, while GAT was better for **fine-grained fraud-heavy micro-clusters**.  

---

## 🔑 Why This Matters  
- Demonstrates that **GNN autoencoders can learn unsupervised fraud representations** directly from tabular data converted into graphs.  
- Shows **GCN vs GAT differences**:  
  - GCN excels at global separation under homophily.  
  - GAT uncovers nuanced local fraud patterns.  
- Provides a **dual-track framework**: supervised models for production-ready baselines, unsupervised embeddings for exploratory fraud analysis.  

---

##  My Contributions & Skills Demonstrated  
- Designed and implemented **custom GNN-based autoencoders** for tabular fraud data.  
- Built an **end-to-end dual-track pipeline** (supervised + unsupervised).  
- Applied **graph construction and representation learning** to a non-graph domain.  
- Benchmarked models with **imbalance-aware evaluation**.  
- Analyzed and explained **why embeddings reveal fraud structure** (homophily, manifold smoothing).  

---

##  Technologies Used  
- **Python** (NumPy, Pandas, Scikit-learn, Imbalanced-learn)  
- **LightGBM** (supervised baseline)  
- **PyTorch / PyTorch Geometric** (custom GAT/GCN autoencoders)  
- **Clustering**: HDBSCAN, KMeans  
- **Visualization**: Matplotlib, Seaborn  
- **Reproducibility**: seed setting, structured experiment notebooks  

---

##  Project Structure (Suggested)  
- `supervised_models.ipynb` → Decision Tree + LightGBM experiments.  
- `gnn_autoencoders.ipynb` → Graph construction, GAT/GCN AE training.  
- `clustering_embeddings.ipynb` → HDBSCAN / KMeans evaluation.  

---

##  Impact  
This project shows how **supervised and unsupervised fraud detection pipelines** complement each other:  
- **Supervised models** (LightGBM) deliver **state-of-the-art predictive performance** with tuning.  
- **Unsupervised custom GNN autoencoders** reveal **fraud communities** in embeddings, offering interpretable and flexible fraud analysis tools.  

---

# Cluster-Driven Churn Modeling with Custom GNNs  

##  Objective  
The primary objective of this project was to **design and evaluate new custom Graph Neural Network (GNN) architectures** and test their effectiveness on a well-known benchmark dataset.  

To ground the study, I used the **Telco Customer Churn dataset** as a standard real-world test case. The project explored how **clustering techniques** could be incorporated into GNN pipelines as an additional relational prior, and whether this would lead to measurable improvements over vanilla GAT/GCN baselines.  

---

##  Project Overview  
Customer churn prediction is a key challenge for subscription-based businesses. Traditional models often fail to capture hidden community structures in customer behavior, especially when dealing with **imbalanced datasets** (few churners vs many non-churners).  

This project explores **cluster-driven graph learning** to evaluate new GNN architectures on the **Telco Churn dataset (7k+ records)**. The study compares multiple **clustering techniques**, evaluates the right number of clusters (**K**) per method, and proposes a **custom cluster-aware GNN**.  

The findings show that **adding clustering signals** into graph models improves downstream classification—particularly recall and F1-score for the minority churn class—validating the effectiveness of the custom architecture.  

---

##  The Problem  
- How to **test the effectiveness of custom GNN architectures** on a standard dataset.  
- Vanilla GNNs (GAT/GCN) often ignore hidden community signals in mixed-type tabular data.  
- Customer churn is **imbalanced** and requires better detection of minority classes (churners).  
- Clustering results may differ by model type (flat vs graph), complicating evaluation.  

---

## 💡 The Solution  
- Build a **comparative pipeline** across clustering methods:  
  - **ClusterGAN** (GAN with categorical latent codes)  
  - **k-Prototypes** (mixed numeric + categorical)  
  - **Hierarchical clustering** (Gower distance)  
  - **Latent Class Analysis (LCA)**  
- Select the optimal number of clusters (**K**) per method using internal & external validity indices.  
- Incorporate cluster signals into a **custom GNN architecture** through:  
  - Cluster-aware embeddings.  
  - Edge reweighting (higher weights for same-cluster edges).  
- Benchmark performance against vanilla GCN/GAT and flat models like LightGBM.  

---

## 🛠️ Techniques & Approaches  
- **Data preprocessing**  
  - Dropped IDs, coerced numeric fields, encoded categorical variables.  
  - Held out a unique test set before any class balancing.  
- **Clustering evaluation**  
  - Internal (Silhouette, CH, DB) and external (NMI, ARI, BIC) criteria.  
  - Compared coarse vs fine-grained clusterings (K=2 vs K=4 for ClusterGAN).  
- **Graph learning**  
  - Constructed k-NN graphs from customer features.  
  - Designed **custom GNNs** that integrate clustering into message passing.  
- **Evaluation**  
  - Used **optimistic precision–recall operating point** for fair comparison.  
  - Reported Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 for the churn class.  

---

## 📊 Key Results  
- **Baseline LightGBM**: Acc. 0.73 | Recall (churn) 0.78 | F1 0.61.  
- **Vanilla GAT/GCN**: Recall improved (0.70–0.77), F1 up to 0.67.  
- **Custom GNN + clustering**:  
  - **LCA (K=5)** → Best minority F1 = 0.68, Recall = 0.77.  
  - **ClusterGAN (K=2)** → Strong geometry, F1 = 0.66, Recall = 0.72.  
  - **ClusterGAN (K=4)** → Highest accuracy (0.82) but lower minority recall.  

➡️ **Conclusion**:  
- **Custom GNN architectures** effectively leveraged clustering to outperform vanilla baselines.  
- Best choice depends on model type:  
  - **Flat models** → benefit from label-aligned clusters (LCA K=5, ClusterGAN K=4).  
  - **Graph models** → benefit from compact, geometric clusters (ClusterGAN K=2).  

---

## 🧑‍💻 My Contributions & Skills Demonstrated  
- Designed and tested **custom GNN architectures** beyond off-the-shelf models.  
- Built an **end-to-end experimental framework** (clustering, graph construction, GNN training, evaluation).  
- Applied **comparative clustering analysis** to mixed-type tabular data.  
- Developed **imbalance-aware evaluation protocols** (precision–recall balancing, calibration).  
- Delivered both **technical insights** (graph homophily, cluster alignment) and **practical guidance** (when to use which clustering).  

---

##  Technologies Used  
- **Python** (NumPy, Pandas, Scikit-learn)  
- **PyTorch / PyTorch Geometric** (GCN, GAT, custom GNN)  
- **LightGBM** (baseline)  
- **Clustering frameworks** (ClusterGAN, k-Prototypes, LCA, hierarchical clustering)  
- **Visualization**: Matplotlib, Seaborn  
- **Reproducibility**: Jupyter notebooks, controlled splits  

---

##  Project Structure  
- `churn-clustergan-k-prototype-1.ipynb` → ClusterGAN + k-Prototypes.  
- `churn-hierarchical-gower-and-lca.ipynb` → Hierarchical + LCA.  
- `churn-clustergcn-1.ipynb` → Baseline models, GAT/GCN, custom GNN experiments.  

---

## 🚀 Impact  
This project demonstrates how **custom GNN architectures** can be systematically evaluated on real-world datasets. Using clustering as a relational prior boosted model effectiveness, especially for the minority churn class, proving the value of going beyond standard GAT/GCN designs.

# CIBMTR Survival Analysis — Theory-Backed Kaggle Submission (v1)

**Notebook:** `cibmtr version 1.ipynb`  
**Competition:** *CIBMTR — Equity in Post-HCT Survival Predictions*

---

## 1. Problem

The competition asked participants to **rank patients by post-HCT event-free survival (EFS) risk**, where:

- **Events** = defined adverse outcomes.  
- **Censoring** = incomplete follow-up.  

**Constraints:**

1. Leaderboard scoring was based on **concordance index (C-index)** — a ranking objective.  
2. **Equity** was emphasized — models had to perform fairly across demographic subgroups.  
3. Predictions had to output a **monotone risk score** (ranking preserved under monotone transformations).  

---

## 2. My Solution

I built a **theory-driven pipeline** that integrates survival analysis fundamentals with practical machine learning.

**System Workflow:**

1. **Data audit & preprocessing**  
   - Inspected missingness and distributions.  
   - Dropped constants/near-constants.  

2. **Imputation with PMM (MICE)**  
   - Used Iterative Imputer with Predictive Mean Matching (stochastic donor-based fills).  
   - Preserved variance and categorical coherence.  

3. **Target engineering (Nelson–Aalen cumulative hazard)**  
   - Computed non-parametric cumulative hazard estimates \(\tilde H(t)\).  
   - Used negative cumulative hazard (-\(\tilde H(t)\)) as regression target.  
   - Added small offset for censored rows to improve separability.  

4. **Modeling (LightGBM Regressor)**  
   - Mixed categorical + numeric features.  
   - Trained on (-\(\tilde H(t)\)) with RMSE objective.  
   - Leveraged monotonicity: outputs are valid risk scores for C-index.  

5. **Submission**  
   - Produced `submission.csv` with ID + prediction.  

---

## 3. Techniques & Approaches

- **Nelson–Aalen labels** — non-parametric, assumption-light, censoring-aware.  
- **Margin-based censoring adjustment** — separated censored vs. event cases at equal times.  
- **PMM imputation (MICE)** — preserved distributional fidelity.  
- **Gradient boosting (LightGBM)** — efficient, interpretable, strong on tabular mixed-type data.  
- **Equity awareness** — monotone risk formulation compatible with subgroup fairness evaluation.  

---

## 4. Skills Demonstrated

- **Survival analysis theory** — hazard, cumulative hazard, censoring, concordance.  
- **Applied ML for healthcare data** — handling censored outcomes and subgroup fairness.  
- **Feature engineering & imputation** — robust PMM over simple mean/median.  
- **Modeling tabular data** — LightGBM with categorical handling.  
- **Competition strategy** — aligning targets to leaderboard metric.  

---

## 5. Technologies Used

- **Python 3.11**  
- **pandas, numpy** — data prep.  
- **scikit-learn (Iterative Imputer)** — PMM/MICE imputation.  
- **lifelines (Nelson–Aalen)** — survival estimation.  
- **LightGBM** — modeling.  

---

## 6. Impact

This pipeline provided a **clean, theory-backed baseline** that ranked patients fairly and robustly. It emphasized **interpretability and survival-theory alignment**, while still leveraging modern ML for strong leaderboard performance.

---

# CIBMTR Survival Analysis — Multi-Approach Ensemble (v2)

**Notebook:** `cibmtr version 2.ipynb`  
**Competition:** *CIBMTR — Equity in Post-HCT Survival Predictions*

  **Important Note:** This notebook **builds upon another Kaggle user’s shared approach**, but I made **several important modifications** to adapt and improve it for my workflow. Unlike v1 (entirely my own design), this solution is partly borrowed but meaningfully extended.

---

## 1. Problem

Same competition context as v1:

1. Rank patients by risk using **C-index**.  
2. Maintain **equitable performance** across subgroups.  
3. Blend **multiple signals** for robustness.  

---

## 2. My Solution

This version explored **three complementary pipelines** and blended them via **rank-based ensembling** to improve performance.

**System Workflow:**

### Approach A — My Implementation (PRL-NN with censoring-aware ranking)
- Designed and implemented an **event-masked Pairwise Ranking Neural Network (PRL-NN)**.  
- **Features:**  
  - Pairwise hinge loss with censoring-aware masks.  
  - Auxiliary time-prediction head (for event-only rows).  
  - Race-wise variance penalty to improve subgroup fairness.  
  - Event-probability classifier mask (XGBoost) to sharpen predictions.  
- **Outputs:** `submission2.csv`.  

### Approach B — Adapted from another Kaggle user (modified Yunbase-style ensemble)
- Started from a shared pipeline, but made **key changes and refinements**:  
  - Adjusted feature handling and time transforms.  
  - Modified subgroup KM-based targets.  
  - Tweaked weighting scheme for subgroup balance.  
- **Models:** LightGBM + CatBoost blend.  
- **Outputs:** `submission1.csv`.  

### Approach C — Multi-target survival ensemble (my extension)
- Combined **four survival signals**:  
  1. Cox partial hazard.  
  2. Kaplan–Meier survival \(S(t)\).  
  3. Nelson–Aalen cumulative hazard (-\(\tilde H(t)\)).  
  4. Signed time (+t for events, -t for censored).  
- Trained multiple **CatBoost** and **LightGBM** regressors per target.  
- **Outputs:** `submission3.csv`.  

### Final Rank Ensemble
- Converted all model predictions to **ranks**.  
- Blended them with tuned weights to get **final `submission.csv`**.  

---

## 3. Techniques & Approaches

- **Pairwise ranking neural network** — directly optimized for C-index.  
- **Subgroup-aware targets & fairness penalties** — ensured equity.  
- **Multi-target survival learning** — captured complementary risk signals.  
- **Rank-based ensembling** — robust to calibration mismatches, aligned with leaderboard metric.  
- **Code adaptation & modification** — carefully adapted another user’s shared code to fit my improved workflow.  

---

## 4. Skills Demonstrated

- **Neural survival modeling** — designing pairwise ranking loss functions.  
- **Fairness-aware ML** — subgroup penalty integration.  
- **Ensembling** — blending heterogeneous models into robust final predictions.  
- **Code adaptation & extension** — responsibly reusing shared Kaggle solutions with meaningful modifications.  
- **Competition strategy** — building multiple diverse pipelines and ensembling for leaderboard gain.  

---

## 5. Technologies Used

- **Python 3.11**  
- **pandas, numpy**  
- **PyTorch Lightning** — neural net implementation.  
- **XGBoost** — event-probability classifier.  
- **LightGBM, CatBoost** — gradient boosting models.  
- **lifelines** — CoxPH, Kaplan–Meier, Nelson–Aalen targets.  

---

## 6. Impact

Compared to v1, this **ensemble approach** achieved **stronger leaderboard results** by:

1. Directly optimizing C-index (via PRL-NN).  
2. Leveraging **multiple survival signals** instead of a single target.  
3. Integrating **fairness explicitly** through penalties and subgroup-aware targets.  

It demonstrates my ability to:  
- **Design original models** (Approach A, C).

68cc4a63125483f14a563233.title: Synthetic Data Augmentation using CTGAN
68cc4a63125483f14a563233.description: This repository documents an extensive set of experiments to generate synthetic data for a benchmark dataset(telco customer churn dataset using CTGAN.
68cc4a63125483f14a563233.detailedContent:
# Synthetic Data Augmentation with CTGAN – Experiments, Results & Diagnosis  

##  Objective  
The purpose of this project was to **implement the CTGAN paper** on the **Telco Customer Churn dataset** to test its ability for **data augmentation** and evaluate whether the generated synthetic samples preserved the statistical and structural properties of the original data.  

---

##  Project Overview  
GANs for tabular data, particularly **CTGAN (Conditional Tabular GAN)**, are often proposed as strong methods for synthetic data generation. To validate this, I implemented CTGAN on the churn dataset and conducted a **comprehensive evaluation** of the generated data, with special attention to numeric features (`MonthlyCharges`, `TotalCharges`, and `tenure`).  

Despite extensive tuning and experimentation, the results showed that **CTGAN fails to faithfully reproduce numeric distributions and their relationships**, revealing important limitations of the model in real-world tabular contexts.  

---

##  The Problem  
- The churn dataset mixes **categorical and continuous features**, with charges and tenure exhibiting strong structural patterns.  
- **MonthlyCharges** is *hyper-multimodal* (hundreds of underlying modes from tariffs and add-ons).  
- **TotalCharges** is **formula-driven** (`≈ tenure × MonthlyCharges`), which CTGAN cannot enforce.  
- CTGAN’s internal Gaussian mixture normalization is not suited for this level of multimodality.  

---

##  Experiments & Solution Attempts  
I tested CTGAN under a wide variety of configurations and preprocessing strategies:  

1. **Baseline CTGAN + Optuna tuning** → varied epochs, embedding dims, architectures, learning rates.  
2. **Discriminator tests (LightGBM)** → consistently achieved very high accuracy (sometimes 1.0) in distinguishing real vs synthetic rows.  
3. **Distribution diagnostics** → KS and Wasserstein tests revealed large numeric deviations.  
4. **Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM)** → revealed extreme multimodality (e.g., `MonthlyCharges` ≈ 998 modes).  
5. **Transformations (log, Box-Cox, Yeo-Johnson, QuantileTransformer)** → normalized marginals but failed to restore conditional/joint fidelity.  
6. **Segmentation strategies** → per-tenure CTGANs (72 splits) and binning, which fragmented data and remained unrealistic.  
7. **Utility tests (TSTR/TSFR)** → mixed results (AUC ≈ 0.817).  
8. **Scaling & post-processing** → rounding/clipping improved realism superficially but didn’t resolve structural flaws.  

---

##  Key Results  
- **QualityReport (best run)**: Shapes 95.78%, Pair Trends 92.71%.  
- **Discriminator test**: Accuracy = 1.0 (perfect separation); another run = 0.91, ROC AUC = 0.78.  
- **KS/Wasserstein**: Large deviations for numeric features.  
- **Utility (TSTR/TSFR)**: AUC ≈ 0.817, Acc ≈ 0.77.  

 **Conclusion**: CTGAN could not faithfully model numeric variables like `MonthlyCharges` and `TotalCharges`. Discriminator models repeatedly proved that synthetic samples were distinguishable from real ones.  

---

##  Diagnosis  
- **MonthlyCharges is hyper-multimodal** → CTGAN not designed for thousands of modes.  
- **TotalCharges is formula-driven** → arithmetic relationships lost in synthetic data.  
- **Conditional heterogeneity** (contract, add-ons) was blurred.  
- **Marginal transformations** were inadequate to fix joint/conditional failures.  

---

##  My Contributions & Skills Demonstrated  
- Implemented the **CTGAN paper** end-to-end for synthetic augmentation.  
- Designed a **multi-layer evaluation pipeline** (statistical tests, discriminators, utility checks).  
- Applied **advanced diagnostics** (GMM, KS/Wasserstein, skewness, kurtosis).  
- Identified and explained **failure modes** of CTGAN on numeric-heavy features.  
- Proposed **future directions with alternative models**.  

---

##  Technologies Used  
- **Python** (NumPy, Pandas, Scikit-learn, Optuna)  
- **SDV / CTGAN library**  
- **LightGBM** (discriminator, utility models)  
- **Statistical tools**: KS tests, Wasserstein, GMM, skewness/kurtosis  
- **Visualization**: Matplotlib, Seaborn  
- **Experiment reproducibility**: Jupyter notebooks with structured experiments  

---

##  Future Work – Alternatives to CTGAN  
Given the repeated failures of CTGAN on numeric fidelity, the next phase is to evaluate alternative generative models:  
- **GaussianCopula** → strong on continuous marginals & dependencies.  
- **TVAE (Tabular VAE)** → better suited for continuous variables than GANs.  
- **Diffusion models for tabular data** → naturally capture multimodality.  
- **Hybrid pipelines** → categorical features with GAN, numeric with copula/diffusion.  

---

##  Impact  
This project demonstrates that **implementing CTGAN directly on churn data is insufficient for realistic numeric modeling**, despite promising quality metrics. It provides a **diagnostic framework** for synthetic data evaluation and highlights the importance of exploring **alternative generative approaches** for numeric-heavy datasets.

68c99091256ed334d8723278.title: Indian Real Estate Price Pipeline
68c99091256ed334d8723278.description: Goal. Build a fully reproducible pipeline that scrapes listings from popular Indian real-estate portals, constructs a clean, analysis-ready dataset, performs exploratory analysis and outlier handling, and trains models to power a price (monthly rent) estimator.
68c99091256ed334d8723278.detailedContent:
Objective: Build a fully reproducible pipeline that scrapes Indian real-estate listings, cleans and structures the data, analyzes pricing patterns, and trains machine learning models to power a rent calculator tool.

Approach & Techniques:

Data Collection: Automated property listing extraction with Selenium, handling infinite scroll and dynamic content.

Data Processing: Built structured datasets (.csv/.json), standardized categorical/numeric fields, and applied EDA with outlier trimming.

Modeling: Trained regression models including Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and a Keras Neural Network using features like location, size, furnishing status, and building age.

Pipeline Design: Implemented an sklearn preprocessing + modeling pipeline with imputation, one-hot encoding, and a reusable predict_rent() function (rent calculator).

Results:

Successfully created a city-wide rental dataset for Bangalore.

Delivered a working rent prediction tool that estimates monthly rents based on property features.

Achieved meaningful baseline performance (MAE in rent prediction; exact metrics to be updated after runs).

Learnings:

Handling dynamic web pages (infinite scroll, JS-rendered data) requires robust scraping strategies with retries, waits, and anti-ban measures.

EDA with quantile-based trimming improves downstream modeling stability in heavy-tailed markets like real estate.

Tree ensembles (RF/GBR) work reliably for heterogeneous tabular data, while neural networks need careful scaling and tuning.

A structured, modular pipeline (scraping → cleaning → EDA → modeling) makes the project extensible to new cities and portals.

68c98cc0256ed334d8723264.title: Credit Score Prediction with XAI techniques
68c98cc0256ed334d8723264.description: Credit Score Prediction with XAI — Built a high-accuracy credit score regressor from 304 numeric features using rigorous missing-data analysis (MCAR/MAR/MNAR), MICE imputation, feature selection (RFE), and strong baselines with LightGBM. To ensure interpretability and compliance, also trained a Neural Monotonic Additive Model (NMAM) with monotonic constraints, and applied Explainable AI (SHAP/TreeSHAP, partials, and local/global attributions) for transparent insights.
68c98cc0256ed334d8723264.detailedContent:
Objective: Develop a reliable machine learning pipeline to predict continuous credit scores from 304 numeric features while ensuring fairness, interpretability, and compliance with domain rules.

Approach & Techniques:

Conducted missing-data diagnostics (MCAR/MAR/MNAR) and applied MICE (Iterative Imputer) to handle large-scale missingness robustly.

Built a LightGBM baseline model, tuned for accuracy and regularization, and applied Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) for feature selection.

Designed a Neural Monotonic Additive Model (NMAM) to enforce monotonic relationships on key drivers (e.g., higher income should not lower scores).

Applied Explainable AI (XAI) methods including SHAP / TreeSHAP, global feature importance, and local instance explanations to ensure transparent decision-making.

Results:

LightGBM achieved MAE ≈ 17 and R² ≈ 0.96 on a 20k hold-out validation set, setting a strong performance benchmark.

NMAM underperformed slightly in raw metrics but demonstrated valuable monotonic interpretability for policy and compliance contexts.

Learnings:

Tree-based ensembles (LightGBM) remain highly effective for numeric tabular data when combined with rigorous imputation.

Monotonic neural models are powerful for regulatory transparency, even if accuracy trade-offs exist.

XAI techniques (SHAP, monotone partials) are crucial not only for interpretability but also for building stakeholder trust in high-stakes domains like credit scoring.
